newsitem.title: UK: UK funds switch to gilts before budget axe falls.
newsitem.headline: UK funds switch to gilts before budget axe falls.

text.p: British fund managers are running investment books with a bias towards gilts in the runup to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's Wednesday budget, but are wary of being caught off balance by surprises.

Portfolio managers expect Wednesday's budget speech to bring changes to mortgage interest relief (MIRAS) and a windfall tax on utilities, but are focused on a widely-tipped change to the Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT) credit enjoyed by tax-exempt investors.

If the ACT credit is cut, "Clearly relative values of gilts and equities will shift somewhat in favour of gilts," said Andrew Hartley, who as head of UK equities at Scottish Equitable controls a portfolio of more than five billion stg.

Tax-exempt institutions, such as pension funds and charities, are currently allowed to claim back a credit on the 20 percent tax paid on company dividends, and if this is phased out or eliminated they will have less incentive to hold shares, fund managers say.

With tax-tree investors estimated as holding 30 percent of shares, Hartley thinks that the abolition of the ACT credit would hit British shares by six or seven percent, but cautions that much of that loss has already been factored in.
"We are heavier relatively in UK fixed interest versus equities but are neutral on UK assets as a whole."
"I think there could be a knee-jerk reaction loss of two or three percent on the day but to push the boat out too far on speculation ahead of the budget is mistaken," he said.
A likely scenario is a phased reduction over a period of years, says James de Sausmarez, director of Henderson Investors.

"The market has discounted an awful lot of a phased withdrawal but all other things being equal gilts will be more attractive relative to equities than they were before," said Stuart Fowler, head of equities at Kleinwort Benson Investment Management.
This will be compounded, Fowler said, by new a regulation on pension fund solvency, the Minimum Funding Requirement (MFR), which makes pension funds more likely to hold gilts as their members age.
One institutional investor who declined to be named sees potentially a 10 percent fall in equities over a short time if the ACT credit is cut all at once.
As a defensive measure, he is running a portfolio that is overweight both in cash and gilts.
But even the abolition of the ACT credit would not spell doom for British stocks, most fund managers say.
In historic terms British equities are fairly cheap in comparison to gilts, according to Hartley.
"There is not an awful lot of mileage for gilts to outperform," he said.
And a budget-prompted correction in shares would quickly find a floor, Hartley added.
"Institutions will see it as a buying opportunity. There is still plenty of cash in institutional coffers and that very well may find its way back in if there is a setback in equities," he said.
But some companies could be hit.
In general, a cut in the ACT credit will be felt more in shares of companies with high-yields and low dividend covers, Hartley said.

Companies with large pension funds relative to their market capitalisation and ageing workforces could find themselves with pension fund shortfalls that eat into profits, according to a study by BZW's Richard Kersley.
He estimates that the funds needed to make up the gap could equal two or three percent of the profits of the FTSE 100.
A reduction in MIRAS is widely anticipated by fund managers, who see it as likely to cool the property market but not to have much of an effect on either shares of gilts.

The elimination of the pension fund tax credit for high rate earners is also seen as a strong bet and a factor that would tend to reduce institutional funds under management, but only in the long term.
Though a certainty, the windfall tax on utilities is seen as too unpredictable in implementation for any big bets to be made, fund managers said.
One fund manger is hoping for nothing more than no major surprises on Wednesday.
Fowler of Kleinwort Benson wants to see a high correlation between press speculation about the budget and the real thing.
"So far Brown has handled himself well, but if they are not managing the news properly that will make life for us extremely uncomfortable."
